newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon must follow corporate cuts, Cohen says.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon must follow corporate cuts, Cohen says.

text.p: The Pentagon is wasting billions of dollars on unnecessary paperwork and bureaucracy, and must follow the cost-cutting course of corporate America, Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Monday.

In a Pentagon speech, Cohen predicted that a major review of U.S. military strategy and forces will, over the next three years, shrink cumbersome regulations in defence business practices and shut down unnecessary civilian support offices.

"By the turn of the century, the department will not be the same organisation it is today," he said in the address to Pentagon workers honouring public service. "We have got to find ways that we can do things better and cheaper and faster."

The Defence Department's Quadrennial Defence Review (QDR) will be sent to Congress on May 15. It is planned as a major blueprint to preserve a superpower military and modernise weapons with limited military funding.
Cohen noted that U.S. industries, such as automobile makers, changed in recent years to become more efficient and competetive in world markets. He said the Pentagon must follow suit.
"We've got to learn from them how we've got to apply some of that -- at least to the Department of Defence," Cohen told the Pentagon officials and civilian workers.

"We can become more efficient, so that we don't have 1,300 pages of regulations, so that we don't have 14 pages of regulations describing a chocolate chip cookie ... for not having offices that are long overdue in terms of their abolition," he added.
Cohen declined to outline what specific changes in civilian bureaucracy, force structure or weapons programmes would be called for in the Quadrennial Defence Review.
But he complained of the time and costs dictated by hundreds of pages of Defence Department rules on purchasing services or obtaining reimbursement for travel expenses.
Cohen suggested, for example, that department credit cards could be used in buying services of less than $2,500 instead of submitting complicated, time-consuming cost vouchers.
He estimated that a billion dollars a year could be saved in simplifying complicated travel reimbursement regulations.
"We really have to find ways to shed systems that we've had around for too long as far as the paperwork is concerned in this building," He said.

"We purchase a lot of goods and services during the course of a year. About 75 percent of those purchases are under $2,500. And yet we're not using the credit card enough in which to acquire those services," he added.
Cohen said one U.S. military daycare centre in Europe last year ordered roughly $1,200 worth of candies and other types of surprises and decorations for a party.

"Yet they didn't use a credit card. They, in fact, filled out a contract that was 11 pages long with some 26 separate accounting lines, which ended up costing almost $1,200 in terms of the accounting audit," he told officials.
"So we spent as much to review it as to acquire it. We could have had it for about 2 percent if we had used a credit card."
